theme: No other gospel; Paul’s apostleship; justification by faith
readingInstruction: Read Galatians 1:1-2:21. This is Paul’s most urgent letter. Notice that he skips the usual thanksgiving and goes straight to alarm. Read his defense of the gospel and of his apostleship, and end with 2:15-21, the heart of the matter.
settingTheScene: Galatians is probably Paul’s earliest letter, written around AD 48 to 49 to churches he founded in the region of Galatia (in modern Turkey). After he left, teachers came who insisted that Gentile believers must be circumcised and keep the law of Moses to be truly part of God’s people. Paul sees that this is not a minor disagreement but a different gospel. The letter is his passionate defense of salvation by grace through faith in Christ alone. It was Martin Luther’s favorite letter, and he called it his “Katie von Bora.”
observation: “Who gave himself for our sins to deliver us from the present evil age, according to the will of our God and Father” (1:4).
“I am astonished that you are so quickly deserting him who called you in the grace of Christ and are turning to a different gospel” (1:6).
“But even if we or an angel from heaven should preach to you a gospel contrary to the one we preached to you, let him be accursed” (1:8).
“For I did not receive it from any man, nor was I taught it, but I received it through a revelation of Jesus Christ” (1:12).
“I opposed him to his face, because he stood condemned” (2:11).
“Yet we know that a person is not justified by works of the law but through faith in Jesus Christ” (2:16).
“I have been crucified with Christ. It is no longer I who live, but Christ who lives in me” (2:20).
“I do not nullify the grace of God, for if righteousness were through the law, then Christ died for no purpose” (2:21).
interpretation:
Paul opens by stressing that he is an apostle “not from men nor through man, but through Jesus Christ and God the Father, who raised him from the dead.” His authority and message come from Christ. Even his greeting contains the gospel: Christ “gave himself for our sins to deliver us from the present evil age.” Then, instead of a thanksgiving, he says, “I am astonished.” The Galatians are deserting the one who called them in grace. There is no other gospel, only some who trouble you and want to distort the gospel of Christ. He pronounces a curse on anyone, even an angel, who preaches a different gospel. This is strong language because the gospel is not negotiable.

He defends his own gospel by telling his story. He once persecuted the church violently and was advancing in Judaism beyond many of his peers. But God, who had set him apart from his mother’s womb, was pleased to reveal his Son to him. He did not consult with flesh and blood, but went to Arabia and returned to Damascus. Three years later he visited Peter in Jerusalem for fifteen days; he met James, the Lord’s brother. The churches of Judea glorified God because of him.

After fourteen years, he went again to Jerusalem with Barnabas and Titus, and laid before the leaders the gospel he preached among the Gentiles. The leaders added nothing to him. Titus, though a Greek, was not compelled to be circumcised. James, Cephas, and John gave Paul and Barnabas the right hand of fellowship, agreeing that Paul was to go to the Gentiles and they to the circumcised, asking only that they remember the poor.

Then the confrontation at Antioch. Peter had eaten with Gentile believers, but when certain men came from James, he drew back and separated himself, fearing the circumcision party. Even Barnabas was led astray. Paul opposed Peter to his face, because his conduct was not in step with the truth of the gospel. This is the principle: the gospel governs how we live together, and it applies even to apostles.

The center of the chapter is 2:15 to 21. “A person is not justified by works of the law but through faith in Jesus Christ.” Paul says this three times in a single verse. Then the personal confession: “I have been crucified with Christ. It is no longer I who live, but Christ who lives in me. And the life I now live in the flesh I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself for me.” This is the verse of the unit. Christ’s death is my death; his life is my life. And Paul concludes: to go back to the law is to say that Christ died for no purpose. The cross either is enough or it is nothing.
connection: Romans 1:16-17 and 3:21-31 explain the same gospel at greater length. Acts 9:1-30, 15:1-35, and 11:27-30 are the background. Genesis 12:3 and 15:6 stand behind chapter 3. Philippians 3:2-9 repeats the warning against confidence in the flesh. 2 Corinthians 11:4 speaks of a different gospel. 1 Timothy 1:15 shows the heart of the gospel. 1 Corinthians 15:1-11 gives its content. Ephesians 2:8-10 sums up salvation by grace.
application:
Memorize Galatians 2:20. Say it each morning this week.

Ask whether you are adding anything to Christ as a requirement for acceptance with God or with his people.

Pray for courage to speak up as Paul did when the gospel is at stake.
prayerPrompts: Thank God for the gospel of grace.
Ask him to keep you from any other gospel.
Thank Jesus for giving himself for your sins.
